{{Short description|Positive integer that is the product of three distinct prime numbers}}

In [[number theory]], a '''sphenic number''' (from {{langx|grc|σφήν}}, 'wedge') is a [[natural number|positive integer]] that is the [[Product (mathematics)|product]] of three distinct [[prime number]]s.{{r|gupta2025|p=147}}{{r|mathworld}} For example, since 2, 3, and 73 are all prime, 438 is a sphenic number because {{math|2 {{times}} 3 {{times}} 73 {{=}} 438}}.{{r|gupta2025|p=147}} Because there are [[Euclid's theorem|infinitely many prime numbers]], there are also infinitely many sphenic numbers.

==Definition==
A sphenic number is a product {{mvar|pqr}} where {{mvar|p}}, {{mvar|q}}, and {{mvar|r}} are three distinct prime numbers.{{r|mathworld}} In other words, the sphenic numbers are the [[Square-free integer|square-free]] 3-[[almost prime]]s.

==Examples==
The smallest sphenic number is {{math|30 {{=}} 2 {{times}} 3 {{times}} 5}}, the product of the smallest three primes.
The first few sphenic numbers are
:[[30 (number)|30]], [[42 (number)|42]], [[66 (number)|66]], [[70 (number)|70]], [[78 (number)|78]], [[102 (number)|102]], [[105 (number)|105]], [[110 (number)|110]], [[114 (number)|114]], [[130 (number)|130]], [[138 (number)|138]], [[154 (number)|154]], [[165 (number)|165]], ... {{OEIS|id=A007304}}

The largest known sphenic number at any time can be obtained by multiplying together the three [[largest known prime]]s.

==Divisors==
All sphenic numbers have exactly eight divisors.{{r|mathworld}} If we express the sphenic number as {{math|n {{=}} p {{times}} q {{times}} r}}, where {{mvar|p}}, {{mvar|q}}, and {{mvar|r}} are distinct primes, then the set of divisors of {{mvar|n}} will be:

:<math>\left\{ 1, \ p, \ q, \ r, \ pq, \ pr, \ qr, \ n \right\}.</math>{{r|mathworld}}

The converse does not hold. For example, 24 is not a sphenic number, but it has exactly eight divisors.

==Properties==
All sphenic numbers are by definition [[Square-free integer|squarefree]], because the prime factors must be distinct.

The [[Möbius function]] of any sphenic number is [[-1|&minus;1.]]

The [[cyclotomic polynomials]] <math>\Phi_n(x)</math>, taken over all sphenic numbers ''n'', may contain arbitrarily large coefficients<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Lehmer |first=Emma |author-link=Emma Lehmer  |date=June 1936 |title=On the magnitude of the coefficients of the cyclotomic polynomial |url=https://projecteuclid.org/journals/bulletin-of-the-american-mathematical-society/volume-42/issue-6/On-the-magnitude-of-the-coefficients-of-the-cyclotomic-polynomial/bams/1183498920.full |journal=Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society |volume=42 |issue=6 |pages=389-392  }}</ref> (for ''n'' a product of two primes the coefficients are <math>\pm 1</math> or 0).

Any multiple of a sphenic number (except by 1) is not sphenic. This is easily provable by the multiplication process at a minimum adding another prime factor, or raising an existing factor to a higher power.

==Consecutive sphenic numbers==
The first case of two consecutive sphenic integers is {{math|230 {{=}} 2 {{times}} 5 {{times}} 23}} and {{math|231 {{=}} 3 {{times}} 7 {{times}} 11}}. The first case of three is {{math|1309 {{=}} 7 {{times}} 11 {{times}}  17}}, {{math|1310 {{=}} 2 {{times}} 5 {{times}} 131}}, and {{math|1311 {{=}} 3 {{times}} 19 {{times}} 23}}. There is no case of more than three, because every fourth consecutive positive integer is divisible by {{math|4 {{=}} 2 {{times}} 2}} and therefore not squarefree {{OEIS|id=A291466}}.

The numbers {{math|2013 {{=}} 3 {{times}} 11 {{times}} 61}}, {{math|2014 {{=}} 2 {{times}} 19 {{times}} 53}}, and {{math|2015 {{=}} 5 {{times}} 13 {{times}} 31}} are all sphenic. The next three consecutive sphenic years will be {{math|2665 {{=}} 5 {{times}} 13 {{times}} 41}}, {{math|2666 {{=}} 2 {{times}} 31 {{times}} 43}} and {{math|2667 {{=}} 3 {{times}} 7 {{times}} 127}} {{OEIS|id=A165936}}.
